papers/paper-15.pdf.subtitle: Toward a Theory of Generative Relational Wealth
papers/paper-15.pdf.teaser: What is wealth — a gold ring, a bride-price, or a shared life? This paper argues the answer is ontological, not economic, and develops “Generative Relational Wealth”: wealth that belongs to the “between” of a couple, is produced by their co-evolution, and — unlike money — is not depleted by use but may be augmented by it.
papers/paper-15.pdf.background: Money and wealth pervade intimate life — bride-price, dowry, gold, the shared household — yet the question of what wealth actually is in a relationship is usually answered in economic terms. The major traditions of wealth theory (mercantilism, classical political economy, Marx's commodity fetishism, Federici's social reproduction, Sen's capabilities, Mauss's gift economy, Eglash's generative justice) each illuminate part of the picture and miss part of it. This paper, Paper XV of the series, takes the question seriously as an ontological one and extends the series' eudaimonics (Paper XIV) and generativity theory (Paper IX) into the domain of political economy. What is at stake is whether the form of wealth that organises a relationship lets the partners genuinely exist as co-evolving subjects, or structurally reduces one or both to exchangeable units within a system of accumulation.
papers/paper-15.pdf.approach: The paper is political-economic and polyphonic. It first maps the major wealth-theory traditions, showing what each illuminates and what it misses about intimate wealth; it then examines how traditional wealth forms (bride-price, gold, dowry) embed intimate relations in power-structured logics of accumulation, and how three mechanisms — settlement, commodification, and indebtedness — foreclose genuine co-evolution. Against this it defines Generative Relational Wealth (GRW) and its self-generating cycle. A central chapter analyses the “happiness jar” — a thought experiment and practice in which couples record and process shared moments of happiness — as a case study in GRW accumulation, depletion-resistance, and regeneration, reading it through semiotics (Peirce's index, Benjamin's aura), psychoanalysis (Lacanian drive theory, the objet petit a), and theoretical physics (relational STDP, phase-space reconstruction, the Δ between symbolic and real registers). It advances a clearly-marked speculative conjecture — that an operator O(x) ∼ x′ generates a non-zero relational remainder ℛ(O(x), x) ≠ 0 — as the source of GRW's inexhaustibility, and develops feminist, psychoanalytic, epistemic-justice, and Hegelian-Marxist perspectives, closing with ethics, cross-cultural and empirical dimensions, and praxis.
questions: What is wealth — a gold ring, a bride-price, a shared life — and which of these is the truest form of riches in an intimate relation?
Is the question of wealth in intimacy fundamentally economic, or ontological?
Does the form of wealth that organises a relationship determine whether the partners can exist as co-evolving subjects, rather than as exchangeable units of accumulation?
Is there a kind of wealth that is generated by, and belongs to, the relation itself rather than to either individual?
Why would such wealth not be depleted by use — and how could use augment it?
How do bride-price, gold, and dowry embed intimacy in power-structured accumulation, and by what mechanisms (settlement, commodification, indebtedness) do they foreclose co-evolution?
Why can artistic processing of shared memories reignite a withering relational cycle?
What is the source of this wealth's inexhaustibility?
How do feminist, psychoanalytic, epistemic-justice, and Hegelian-Marxist lenses each read it?
What is the dialectical relation between material/symbolic wealth and generative relational wealth?

key_concepts.gloss: Wealth generated through co-evolutionary activity in the relational field, belonging to the “between” rather than to either individual; stored not in any material or symbolic medium but in the permanent structural modifications of the relational attractor landscape.

key_concepts.term: Use does not deplete but may augment
key_concepts.gloss: GRW's most fundamental property: drawing on it does not spend it down, and may instead increase it — the inverse of ordinary, scarce, depletable wealth.
GRW as the “self-fuel” of the relational field: produced by co-evolution and becoming the dynamic condition for further co-evolution, so the cycle spirals rather than merely circles.
Three mechanisms by which traditional wealth forms structurally foreclose genuine relational co-evolution.
A thought experiment and practical paradigm in which couples record and process shared moments of happiness — the paper's case study in GRW accumulation, depletion-resistance, and regeneration.
The clearly-marked speculative conjecture that re-processing a shared memory leaves a non-zero relational remainder — proposed as the source of GRW's inexhaustibility.
GRW read psychoanalytically as wealth that bypasses the symbolic order's power structures, rather than being accumulated within them.

Material and symbolic wealth as necessary condition and secondary aspect; GRW as primary aspect and generative ground — an irreducible relation, since without symbolic wealth GRW cannot be sustained, and without GRW symbolic wealth is ontologically impoverished.

claims: The truest wealth in an intimate relation is an ontological, not an economic, question: the form of wealth organising the relation determines whether the partners exist as co-evolving subjects or are reduced to exchangeable units of accumulation.
Generative Relational Wealth is generated through co-evolutionary activity and belongs to the “between” rather than to either individual.

GRW's defining property is that use does not deplete it but may augment it, because it is stored in the permanent structural modifications of the relational attractor landscape rather than in any material or symbolic medium.
GRW is the self-fuel of the relational field: generated through co-evolution, it becomes the condition for further co-evolution (the generative relational cycle).
Every major tradition of wealth theory illuminates something, and misses something, about wealth in intimate relations.

Traditional wealth forms (bride-price, gold, dowry) embed intimacy in power-structured accumulation, and the mechanisms of settlement, commodification, and indebtedness structurally foreclose genuine co-evolution.
The happiness jar shows GRW accumulating, resisting depletion, and regenerating; artistic processing of shared memories can reignite a withering relational cycle.
(Speculative, explicitly marked) The operator O(x) ∼ x′ generates a non-zero structural remainder ℛ(O(x), x) ≠ 0 that is the source of GRW's inexhaustibility.
GRW is structurally non-phallic wealth that bypasses the symbolic order's power structures; care labour is its primary production mechanism and relational subjectivity its highest form.
Recognition of epistemic asymmetry in intimate relations is a condition for GRW generation.
The dialectic of material wealth (necessary condition, secondary aspect) and GRW (primary aspect, generative ground) is irreducible.
papers/paper-15.pdf.conclusion: Reframing wealth in intimate life as ontological, the paper argues that the truest riches are not the gold ring or the bride-price but the co-evolved structure of a shared life — wealth that belongs to the “between,” that is produced by the partners' co-evolution, and that use augments rather than depletes. Having mapped the wealth-theory traditions, named the mechanisms that foreclose co-evolution, worked through the happiness jar, and developed feminist, psychoanalytic, epistemic-justice, and Hegelian-Marxist readings, it holds that care labour produces GRW, that recognising epistemic asymmetry conditions it, and that material and generative wealth stand in an irreducible dialectic. Its central physics conjecture — the structural remainder — is offered as explicitly speculative. The account extends the series' eudaimonics (Paper XIV) and generativity theory (Paper IX) into political economy and closes with praxis and an envoi.
contributions: The concept of Generative Relational Wealth (GRW) — relation-owned, co-evolutionarily produced wealth whose use augments rather than depletes — together with the self-sustaining generative relational cycle.

A critical map of the major wealth-theory traditions (mercantilism, classical political economy, Marx, Federici, Sen, Mauss, Eglash) by what each illuminates and misses about wealth in intimate relations.
An analysis of how bride-price, gold, and dowry embed intimacy in accumulation, via the three foreclosure mechanisms of settlement, commodification, and indebtedness.
The happiness jar as a worked case study in GRW accumulation, depletion-resistance, and regeneration, read through semiotics, psychoanalysis, and theoretical physics.
The clearly-marked speculative structural-remainder conjecture (ℛ(O(x), x) ≠ 0) as a candidate source of GRW's inexhaustibility.

Feminist (non-phallic wealth; care labour as primary production), psychoanalytic, epistemic-justice, and Hegelian-Marxist analyses of GRW, and the irreducible dialectic of material/symbolic wealth and GRW.
Extension of the series' eudaimonics (Paper XIV) and generativity theory (Paper IX) into the domain of political economy.

outline.section: 5. The theory of Generative Relational Wealth
outline.gist: Defines GRW — its location in the “between,” its storage in the relational attractor landscape, its depletion-resistance, the self-generating cycle, and the structural remainder.
Reads the happiness jar through Peirce's index and Benjamin's aura to explain how recorded shared moments carry and regenerate relational value.
Develops the structural correspondence between the relational field and the forms in which GRW is stored and re-activated across registers.
Reads GRW through Lacanian drive theory and the objet petit a, arguing it is structurally non-phallic wealth that bypasses the symbolic order's power structures.
Argues that care labour is GRW's primary production mechanism and relational subjectivity its highest form.
Argues that the recognition of epistemic asymmetry in intimate relations is a condition for GRW generation.
Develops the irreducible dialectic between material/symbolic wealth (necessary condition, secondary aspect) and GRW (primary aspect, generative ground).
Draws out the ethics of GRW — what it asks of partners who would generate and sustain it.
Considers empirical handles on GRW and its variation across cultural forms of intimate wealth.
Turns to practice: how partners might actually generate, protect, and regenerate GRW in daily relational life.
Gathers the argument: wealth in intimate life is ontological, care labour produces it, and material and generative wealth stand in irreducible dialectic.
A closing literary return to the paper's opening image of wealth and the shared life.
